questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Dark-field microscopy reveals motile spirochetes. Which is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) is caused by Treponema pallidum. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the treatment of choice per WHO and CDC guidelines. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old farmer presents with black-grain mycetoma of the foot with swelling and multiple discharging sinuses for 2 years. Microscopy of the grain shows dematiaceous hyphae. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Madurella mycetomatis is the most common cause of black-grain eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma). Nocardia and Actinomadura cause white-grain actinomycetoma. Black grains indicate eumycetoma, most commonly due to Madurella mycetomatis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman has depigmented patches on the face and hands with loss of sensation, and a single skin smear shows 2+ AFB. Slit-skin smear from the ear lobe shows 4+ AFB. What is the correct Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: Borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy has multiple lesions, partial loss of sensation, and high bacillary load (4+ on smear). The discordance between partial tuberculoid features (some anaesthesia) and high smear positivity is characteristic of BL leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal-looking skin and erythematous areas, predominantly on the lower abdomen and inner thighs. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin in elderly patients. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. The target antigen is BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. It is subepidermal in location.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with extensive, thick, hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp, ears, and hands. Microscopy shows thousands of mites. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Combined oral ivermectin and topical permethrin with keratolytics
questions.exp: Norwegian (crusted) scabies in an immunocompromised patient requires combined therapy: oral ivermectin plus topical permethrin along with keratolytics (salicylic acid) to reduce the hyperkeratotic crust and allow penetration of scabicides. Multiple doses of ivermectin (days 1, 2, 8, 9, and 15) are used.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man develops painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the right V2 dermatome. Two days later he develops ipsilateral facial palsy. Which complication has occurred?
questions.exp: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) results from VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII), causing ear pain, vesicles in the external auditory canal/pinna, and facial palsy. V2 involvement with facial palsy points to geniculate ganglion involvement.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with erythema, scaling, and hyperpigmentation in a butterfly distribution over the cheeks and nose, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and alopecia for 6 months. ANA is 1:640 (homogeneous). Which antibody is most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibodies are highly specific (>95%) for SLE, though sensitivity is only 25-30%. Anti-dsDNA is sensitive but less specific. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is seen in Sjogren's and neonatal lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the nasal ala that has been slowly enlarging for 2 years. Which histological finding would be expected?
opts: Squamous pearl formation with individual cell keratinisation
Palisading basaloid cells with peripheral clefting
Reed-Sternberg cells in a lymphocytic background
Pagetoid spread of atypical cells in the epidermis
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) histologically shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral nuclear palisading and artifactual clefting (retraction artifact) between the tumour islands and surrounding stroma. It is the most common skin cancer in fair-skinned individuals.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with episodic well-demarcated erythema on the cheeks triggered by spicy food and heat, along with flushing, tachycardia, and diarrhoea. Urine 5-HIAA is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Carcinoid syndrome results from serotonin-secreting tumours (usually gastrointestinal). Classic triad: flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm. Urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, serotonin metabolite) is the diagnostic test. Skin flushing in carcinoid is episodic and can be bright red or cyanotic.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with annular plaques with a raised erythematous border and central clearing on the trunk. KOH mount shows septate hyphae. Fungal culture grows a dermatophyte producing macroconidia with thin walls and ≤6 cells, with no microconidia. Which species is most likely?
questions.exp: Epidermophyton floccosum produces smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters of 2-3, with 2-5 cells and no microconidia. It causes tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and onychomycosis but NOT tinea capitis. T. rubrum has pencil-shaped macroconidia; M. canis has spindle-shaped macroconidia with thick walls.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with known psoriasis develops erythroderma covering >90% BSA. He is febrile (39°C), has peripheral oedema, and feels unwell. Which immediate management is most appropriate?
opts: Hospital admission, IV fluids, emollients, treat the precipitating cause
questions.exp: Erythrodermic psoriasis is a dermatological emergency with risks of hypothermia, high-output cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia, and sepsis. Immediate management: hospitalisation, IV fluid resuscitation, emollients, temperature regulation, and treatment of the precipitating cause. Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in psoriatic erythroderma as withdrawal may precipitate pustular psoriasis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with haemorrhagic, ulcerated violaceous plaques on the lower limbs associated with bowel symptoms. He is HIV negative. Biopsy shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the most likely type?
questions.exp: Classic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in elderly Mediterranean or Eastern European men, is HIV-negative, slowly progressive, involves the lower limbs, and may involve viscera. It is caused by HHV-8. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces — the classic histology.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with lepromatous leprosy and starts multidrug therapy (MDT). After 3 weeks she develops high fever, erythematous tender nodules on the face, arms, and legs, and joint pain. What is this reaction called?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in LL and BL leprosy, typically after starting MDT. It is an immune complex-mediated reaction (Type III hypersensitivity) characterised by painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic involvement. Managed with thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and dysphagia for 6 months. Her ANA is positive in a nucleolar pattern. Which antibody is most characteristic?
questions.exp: The CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are characteristic of CREST syndrome (70-80% sensitivity). Anti-Scl-70 is seen in diffuse cutaneous SSc with interstitial lung disease. Anti-RNA Pol III predicts renal crisis.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with a vesicular eruption on the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp with intense pruritus. Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae — pathognomonic. Treatment is dapsone for rapid symptom control (within 24-48h) plus strict gluten-free diet for long-term remission. Dapsone does not treat the enteropathy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with multiple hypopigmented macules on the trunk and upper limbs for 3 years. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH mount reveals short hyphae and clusters of spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (a lipophilic yeast). KOH shows the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (short hyphae + round spores). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green/gold fluorescence in active lesions. Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid inhibiting tyrosinase.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a painless, firm, indurated plaque on the face enlarging over months. Biopsy shows tuberculoid granulomas in the superficial dermis without caseation. AFB stain is negative. Mantoux is 20 mm. Diascopy reveals 'apple jelly' nodules. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis in India. It presents as a slowly enlarging reddish-brown plaque on the face with 'apple jelly' nodules on diascopy. Histology shows tuberculoid granulomas (may have caseation), Mantoux is strongly positive but AFB is usually absent due to paucibacillary nature.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with extensive erosions in the mouth and flaccid bullae on the chest and back. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG ('chicken wire' pattern) throughout the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) has autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal dominant, mucocutaneous type) and desmoglein 1 (skin dominant). DIF shows intercellular IgG and C3 in a 'fish-net' or 'chicken wire' pattern. Acantholysis is intraepidermal (suprabasal). BP180 is target in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-negative man presents with three painless genital ulcers and tender, fluctuant inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) that have developed over 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The primary lesion is a small, painless papule/ulcer (often missed). Secondary stage has tender, fluctuant inguinal lymphadenopathy (groove sign if nodes above and below inguinal ligament). Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid (painful ulcer + tender bubo).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for SLE develops bilateral 'bull's eye' maculopathy on OCT. Which monitoring investigation should have been performed regularly from the start?
opts: Visual field testing and optical coherence tomography
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (HCQ retinopathy) with bull's-eye maculopathy. Annual ophthalmological screening with visual field testing (10-2 Humphrey) and OCT is recommended from year 1 if risk factors present, otherwise from year 5. This is the most important toxicity monitoring for HCQ.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with well-defined, scaly erythematous plaques on the scalp, elbows, and lumbosacral region has nail pitting and onycholysis. His son has similar lesions. Which HLA type is strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: HLA-Cw6 is the major genetic susceptibility allele for psoriasis, present in ~50-65% of psoriasis patients vs ~15% of controls. HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis. HLA-DR3 is associated with SLE and DH. HLA-B51 is associated with Behcet disease.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with atopic eczema presents with chronic, relapsing, pruritic dermatitis in flexural areas with markedly elevated serum IgE. Which interleukins primarily drive the Th2-dominated immune response in this condition?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is driven by a Th2 immune response. Key cytokines: IL-4 (drives IgE class switching and Th2 differentiation), IL-13 (impairs barrier function), and IL-31 (major pruritogen). This forms the basis of dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα, blocking both IL-4 and IL-13) as first-line biologic for moderate-severe AD.

questions.q: A 60-year-old immunosuppressed man develops rapidly enlarging, pink, exophytic nodules on the face over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows lobular proliferation of small capillaries with plump endothelial cells and a neutrophilic infiltrate. Warthin-Starry stain is positive. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) is caused by Bartonella henselae (or B. quintana) in immunocompromised patients, particularly HIV-positive individuals. It mimics pyogenic granuloma clinically but histology shows lobular capillary proliferation with plump endothelial cells and a neutrophilic infiltrate. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals the organisms. Treated with azithromycin or doxycycline.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with multiple vesicles and pustules on the face, bullous impetigo on the trunk, and peeling skin at flexures (Nikolsky positive). The child is febrile. Blood cultures are negative. What is the pathogenic mechanism?
opts: Direct bacterial invasion of the skin
Immune complex deposition in the dermis
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II producing exfoliative toxins A and B (ETA/ETB). These toxins specifically cleave desmoglein 1 in the superficial epidermis (granular layer), causing the superficial blistering and skin peeling. Unlike TEN, mucosae are spared.

questions.q: A 65-year-old chronic smoker with significant sun exposure presents with a crusted, slow-growing erythematous scaly plaque on the lower lip for 2 years. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia without dermal invasion. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) of the lip
Actinic cheilitis with SCC in situ
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis affects the lower lip due to chronic sun exposure, presenting as dryness, scaling, and erosions. When full-thickness epidermal dysplasia is present (SCC in situ), it carries a higher risk of progression to invasive SCC than actinic keratosis elsewhere. Treatment: vermilionectomy or CO2 laser ablation.

questions.q: A patient undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent BCC on the nasal tip. What is the principal advantage of this technique over standard excision?
opts: It is faster and less expensive than standard excision
Complete margin examination (100%) allowing maximum tissue conservation
It can be performed under general anaesthesia only
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery allows intraoperative examination of 100% of the surgical margin (horizontal frozen sections) rather than the ~1% sampled in bread-loaf sectioning. This achieves the highest cure rates for BCC/SCC while conserving maximal tissue, critical in cosmetically sensitive areas like the nose, periocular region, and ears.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops butterfly rash, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers after 3 months of hydralazine therapy. ANA positive, anti-histone antibodies positive, anti-dsDNA negative. What should be the first step in management?
questions.exp: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is characterised by anti-histone antibodies and negative anti-dsDNA (unlike SLE). Common culprits: hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF agents. Treatment: withdraw the offending drug — symptoms usually resolve within weeks to months. Symptomatic treatment with HCQ or steroids if needed.

questions.q: Multiple coin-shaped erythematous plaques with scales are seen on the trunk. Auspitz sign is positive on dermoscopy. What is the pathological basis of the Auspitz sign?
opts: Parakeratosis with neutrophilic infiltration causing scale
Thinning of the suprapapillary plate over elongated dermal papillae with dilated capillaries
Loss of the granular layer leading to superficial erosions
questions.exp: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removal of scale) occurs because psoriatic plaques have thinned suprapapillary epidermis over elongated dermal papillae with dilated, tortuous capillary loops. Removing the overlying parakeratotic scale unroofs these capillaries. This corresponds histologically to elongated rete ridges and suprapapillary thinning.

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with a solitary, slowly growing, verrucous plaque on the medial ankle for 3 years. Biopsy shows epidermal hyperplasia and sclerotic fibrous bodies (muriform cells/Medlar bodies) — brown, thick-walled, septate cells dividing by binary fission. What is the most common causative organism in India?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is most commonly caused by Fonsecaea pedrosoi in India (also Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa). Muriform cells (Medlar/sclerotic bodies) are pathognomonic on histology — brown, thick-walled, septate cells dividing by binary fission. It presents as verrucous plaques from traumatic inoculation, commonly on lower limbs.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with diffuse non-scarring hair loss for 6 months. Hair pull test is positive (>6 telogen hairs). TFTs, CBC, serum ferritin, and ANA are all normal. Hair mount shows 80% telogen hairs. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Reassurance and address any reversible trigger
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium is self-limiting hair loss 2-3 months after a triggering event (stress, illness, delivery, dieting). With normal investigations, reassurance is key. The condition resolves spontaneously in 6-12 months. Minoxidil may be considered if shedding persists beyond 6 months. Intralesional steroids are used for alopecia areata, not telogen effluvium.

questions.q: A 19-year-old man presents with a painless genital ulcer that has a clean base and indurated edges. Histology shows plasma cell-rich infiltrate. Serological test for syphilis (VDRL) is reactive at 1:64. Which serological test confirms true syphilis infection rather than a false positive?
questions.exp: Non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) detect cardiolipin antibodies and can be false positive in autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, and infections. Treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS, TPPA) detect antibodies specific to T. pallidum and are used to confirm a reactive non-treponemal test. TPHA remains positive even after treatment (serofast).
